quotes: Nothing in this chapter is a Git feature. Git supplies the commit, the ref and the tag. slides.headline: In one sentence
slides.body: An environment is a named GitHub object that a job can reference, and that holds protection rules the job must pass before it starts, and secrets and variables the job can read only after that.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: A job references an environment with the environment key, either as a name or as a mapping with a name and a URL.

slides.direction: The root-cause box of section 20B.4, one line at a time. Observed behavior: a job that names "production" started without waiting for anybody. Git state: irrelevant; the workflow file names the environment correctly. Mechanism: protection rules are properties of the environment object on GitHub; the environment had been created by the first run that named it, with no rules; or the repository is private on a plan where reviewers do not apply. Root cause: the gate was assumed from the YAML and never configured or verified. Why GitHub does it: naming a missing environment creates it, so that a first deployment works without an administrator; rules are an administrator's decision. Correct fix: configure the rules; read them back with a `gh api` call on the environment. Prevention: create environments before the workflow that uses them; keep their configuration in a reviewed script; test the gate with a harmless run.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : A job that names "production" started without waiting for anybody.
Git state         : Irrelevant. The workflow file names the environment correctly.
Mechanism         : Protection rules are properties of the environment object on GitHub. The
                    environment had been created by the first run that named it, with no rules;
                    or the repository is private on a plan where reviewers do not apply.
Root cause        : The gate was assumed from the YAML and never configured or verified.
Why GitHub does it: Naming a missing environment creates it, so that a first deployment works
                    without an administrator; rules are an administrator's decision.
Correct fix       : Configure the rules; read them back with
                    gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/environments/production.
Prevention        : Create environments before the workflow that uses them; keep their
                    configuration in a reviewed script; test the gate with a harmless run.

Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Assuming a gate from the line environment: production. Root cause: protection rules are properties of the environment object on GitHub, and naming a missing environment creates it without any rule.
A misspelled environment name. Root cause: the misspelling names a new, unprotected environment; there is no error.
Rebuilding in the deploy job. Root cause: a second build is not guaranteed to produce the same bytes, so the deployed thing is not the tested thing.
Re-running an old deploy run. Root cause: a re-run uses the commit of the original run, so it deploys old code over new.
Treating the environment as the only production control. Root cause: it is enforced by GitHub, and credentials that also work from elsewhere bypass it.

slides.body: Let's land this.

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: An environment is a GitHub object; its rules must pass before the job is sent to a runner, and its secrets are readable only after that.
Naming an environment that does not exist creates it without rules, so a gate must be configured and read back, not assumed from YAML.
Build once and pass the artifact: the bytes that were tested are the bytes that ship, checked by a digest.
What a deployment contains is the two-dot range from the deployed commit to the new one, and a deploy script should refuse unless the old commit is an ancestor of the new.
The gate is a ruleset on main, an environment that accepts only main, and a required reviewer; remove any one and there is a path around the other two.

slides.body: Read sections 20B.1 to 20B.4 of Chapter 20B.
You can now say where a production gate really lives, and how to read it back as evidence.

beats.text: Production is the live system that real users depend on, and a commit is one saved snapshot of the project. The textbook's comment on that question is the lesson of this video: the answer isn't in Git. It's in GitHub objects: an environment, its protection rules, a deployment record. If you can't say which rules gate the production job and who can bypass them, you don't control your releases.
beats.tele: Production is the live system that real users depend on, and a commit is one saved snapshot of the project. The textbook's comment on that question is the lesson of this video: the answer isn't in Git. It's in GitHub objects: an environment, its protection rules, a deployment record. If you can't say which rules gate the production job and who can bypass them, you don't control your releases.

beats.text: And here's how a team finds out that it doesn't. The workflow file says environment: production. Everyone has read that line and assumed a gate. One day a deployment goes to production without anyone approving it. The YAML was correct. So what was missing? Take a guess, out loud.
beats.tele: And here's how a team finds out that it doesn't. The workflow file says `environment: production`. Everyone has read that line and assumed a gate. One day a deployment goes to production without anyone approving it. The YAML was correct. So what was missing? Take a guess, out loud.

beats.text: The gate had never been configured, and naming an environment that doesn't exist creates it, without any rule. So what does make a real gate? Three things together, and before this video ends you'll be able to say all three to a CTO.
beats.tele: The gate had never been configured, and naming an environment that doesn't exist creates it, without any rule. So what does make a real gate? Three things together, and before this video ends you'll be able to say all three to a CTO.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A workflow is a file that tells GitHub Actions which jobs to run when an event happens, and a job is a list of steps on one fresh machine, the runner. Chapter 20A taught the parts of a workflow. Chapter 20B uses those parts to deliver software, and this is its first video.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A workflow is a file that tells GitHub Actions which jobs to run when an event happens, and a job is a list of steps on one fresh machine, the runner. Chapter 20A taught the parts of a workflow. Chapter 20B uses those parts to deliver software, and this is its first video.

beats.text: The textbook is firm about the layers here. Nothing in this chapter is a Git feature. Git supplies the commit, the ref and the tag. GitHub Actions decides when to run, on which machine, with which token. And GitHub decides what a "deployment" and a "check" are.
beats.tele: The textbook is firm about the layers here. Nothing in this chapter is a Git feature. Git supplies the commit, the ref and the tag. GitHub Actions decides when to run, on which machine, with which token. And GitHub decides what a "deployment" and a "check" are.

beats.text: Three topics. Environments: what they are, what their rules do, and what you must configure outside the workflow file. Workflow 8, which deploys to staging, the rehearsal system, what was built once. And workflow 9, which promotes the same artifact to production behind an approval. An artifact is a set of files that a job uploads to GitHub.
beats.tele: Three topics. Environments: what they are, what their rules do, and what you must configure outside the workflow file. Workflow 8, which deploys to staging, the rehearsal system, what was built once. And workflow 9, which promotes the same artifact to production behind an approval. An artifact is a set of files that a job uploads to GitHub.

beats.text: Git still earns its place in the demonstration, because three questions about a deployment are Git questions. Are these the same bytes? Which commits am I about to ship? And is this deployment going forwards or backwards?
beats.tele: Git still earns its place in the demonstration, because three questions about a deployment are Git questions. Are these the same bytes? Which commits am I about to ship? And is this deployment going forwards or backwards?

beats.text: The deployments in the labs are simulated. The script prints what it would deploy and changes nothing anywhere.
beats.tele: The deployments in the labs are simulated. The script prints what it would deploy and changes nothing anywhere.

beats.text: Here's what you'll walk away with.
beats.tele: Here's what you'll walk away with.

beats.text: After this video you can:
beats.tele: After this video you can:

beats.text: list what must be configured on GitHub, outside the workflow file, for environment: to protect anything;
beats.tele: list what must be configured on GitHub, outside the workflow file, for `environment:` to protect anything;

beats.text: explain required reviewers, deployment branch rules and environment secrets;
beats.tele: explain required reviewers, deployment branch rules and environment secrets;

beats.tele: explain workflow 8 line by line and say which commit range a deployment contains;

beats.tele: guard a deployment against going backwards.

beats.text: In one sentence. An environment is a named GitHub object that a job can reference, and that holds protection rules the job must pass before it starts, and secrets and variables the job can read only after that. A secret is an encrypted value stored in GitHub's settings.
beats.tele: In one sentence. An environment is a named GitHub object that a job can reference, and that holds protection rules the job must pass before it starts, and secrets and variables the job can read only after that. A secret is an encrypted value stored in GitHub's settings.

beats.text: Precisely. A job references an environment with the environment key, either as a name or as a mapping with a name and a URL. The rules:
beats.tele: Precisely. A job references an environment with the `environment` key, either as a name or as a mapping with a name and a URL. The rules:

beats.text: Required reviewers: the job waits until a listed person or team approves. Up to six users or teams. One approval is enough. And "prevent self-review" stops the person who started the run from approving it.
beats.tele: Required reviewers: the job waits until a listed person or team approves. Up to six users or teams. One approval is enough. And "prevent self-review" stops the person who started the run from approving it.

beats.text: Wait timer: the job waits a fixed time after it is triggered, from 1 to 43,200 minutes, which is 30 days. Waiting isn't billed.
beats.tele: Wait timer: the job waits a fixed time after it is triggered, from 1 to 43,200 minutes, which is 30 days. Waiting isn't billed.

beats.text: Deployment branches and tags: only runs on matching refs may deploy. The choices are "No restriction", "Protected branches only", or "Selected branches and tags". Patterns are matched against the ref, and a star doesn't match a slash.
beats.tele: Deployment branches and tags: only runs on matching refs may deploy. The choices are "No restriction", "Protected branches only", or "Selected branches and tags". Patterns are matched against the ref, and a star doesn't match a slash.

beats.text: Allow administrators to bypass: lets a repository administrator force the deployment. It's on by default and can be switched off per environment.
beats.tele: Allow administrators to bypass: lets a repository administrator force the deployment. It's on by default and can be switched off per environment.

beats.text: Custom deployment protection rules, where a GitHub App decides: public preview.
beats.tele: Custom deployment protection rules, where a GitHub App decides: public preview.

beats.text: Environment secrets: secrets that exist only for jobs that reference the environment, and that aren't readable before a required approval is given. Environment variables: the same scoping, without secrecy.
beats.tele: Environment secrets: secrets that exist only for jobs that reference the environment, and that aren't readable before a required approval is given. Environment variables: the same scoping, without secrecy.

beats.text: Two details decide how safe this is.
beats.tele: Two details decide how safe this is.

beats.text: First: all protection rules must pass before a job that references the environment is sent to a runner. The gate is in front of the machine. It's not a step inside the job that the job could skip.
beats.tele: First: all protection rules must pass before a job that references the environment is sent to a runner. The gate is in front of the machine. It's not a step inside the job that the job could skip.

beats.text: Quick quiz. A workflow names an environment with a typing error in the name. What happens? A, the run stops with an error. B, the job starts, with no gate at all. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. A workflow names an environment with a typing error in the name. What happens? A, the run stops with an error. B, the job starts, with no gate at all. Your answer?

beats.text: B, and that's the second detail. A workflow that names an environment that doesn't exist creates it, without any rule. Anyone who can edit workflows can do that, while only repository administrators can configure an environment. So a typing error in the name gives you an unprotected environment, not an error.
beats.tele: B, and that's the second detail. A workflow that names an environment that doesn't exist creates it, without any rule. Anyone who can edit workflows can do that, while only repository administrators can configure an environment. So a typing error in the name gives you an unprotected environment, not an error.

beats.text: Plan gates. Check these before you design a gate. Required reviewers, wait timers, custom rules and disabling the administrator bypass are available in public repositories on any plan, and in private repositories on Enterprise. They aren't available in private repositories on Free, Pro or Team. Deployment branch and tag rules and environment secrets: public on any plan, private on Pro, Team or Enterprise.
beats.tele: Plan gates. Check these before you design a gate. Required reviewers, wait timers, custom rules and disabling the administrator bypass are available in public repositories on any plan, and in private repositories on Enterprise. They aren't available in private repositories on Free, Pro or Team. Deployment branch and tag rules and environment secrets: public on any plan, private on Pro, Team or Enterprise.

beats.text: Whether a private repository on a Free plan can use environments at all is a conflict inside GitHub's own material. A changelog entry of the fifteenth of May 2025 says environments are available on all plans in public and private repositories. The managing-environments page on the first of October 2026 still says users on Free plans can configure environments only for public repositories.
beats.tele: Whether a private repository on a Free plan can use environments at all is a conflict inside GitHub's own material. A changelog entry of the fifteenth of May 2025 says environments are available on all plans in public and private repositories. The managing-environments page on the first of October 2026 still says users on Free plans can configure environments only for public repositories.

beats.text: The Phase 0 report couldn't resolve it. The practice repository of the labs is public, so the labs aren't affected. For a private repository, test it before you promise a gate.
beats.tele: The Phase 0 report couldn't resolve it. The practice repository of the labs is public, so the labs aren't affected. For a private repository, test it before you promise a gate.

beats.text: Inside .git. Nothing. An environment, its rules, its secrets and the deployment records it produces are GitHub objects. The only trace in Git is the word after environment: in the workflow file. That's why a repository that is mirrored to another host loses its gates, and why the YAML line proves nothing until you've read the environment's settings.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`. Nothing. An environment, its rules, its secrets and the deployment records it produces are GitHub objects. The only trace in Git is the word after `environment:` in the workflow file. That's why a repository that is mirrored to another host loses its gates, and why the YAML line proves nothing until you've read the environment's settings.

beats.text: Creating environments. The documented path in the interface is the repository's settings, then Environments. The same can be done with the REST API, which is what you want for configuration that is reviewed as code.
beats.tele: Creating environments. The documented path in the interface is the repository's settings, then Environments. The same can be done with the REST API, which is what you want for configuration that is reviewed as code.

beats.text: The two reading commands are 🟢 SAFE. gh secret set and gh variable set are 🟡 CAUTION: they overwrite the stored value, and the old secret value can't be read back. gh secret set without --body reads the value from standard input or prompts for it, which keeps it out of your shell history. Never put a real secret value on screen.
beats.tele: The two reading commands are 🟢 SAFE. `gh secret set` and `gh variable set` are 🟡 CAUTION: they overwrite the stored value, and the old secret value can't be read back. `gh secret set` without `--body` reads the value from standard input or prompts for it, which keeps it out of your shell history. Never put a real secret value on screen.

beats.text: The PUT is 🔴 DANGEROUS. Five answers. What it changes: it replaces the environment's protection settings with the body sent. What it can destroy: the previous settings, required reviewers included, which exist nowhere else unless you saved them. How to preview: read the environment with a GET first. How to recover: send the previous configuration again. When it's appropriate: for environment rules kept as code.
beats.tele: The `PUT` is 🔴 DANGEROUS. Five answers. What it changes: it replaces the environment's protection settings with the body sent. What it can destroy: the previous settings, required reviewers included, which exist nowhere else unless you saved them. How to preview: read the environment with a `GET` first. How to recover: send the previous configuration again. When it's appropriate: for environment rules kept as code.

beats.text: Workflow 8: deploying to staging.
beats.tele: Workflow 8: deploying to staging.

beats.text: The build job installs from the lock file, runs the tests, builds, and uploads the artifact.
beats.tele: The `build` job installs from the lock file, runs the tests, builds, and uploads the artifact.

beats.text: The deploy-staging job needs build, names the environment staging with a URL taken from a variable, checks out the repository, downloads the artifact, and runs the deployment script with the token in env.
beats.tele: The `deploy-staging` job needs `build`, names the environment `staging` with a URL taken from a variable, checks out the repository, downloads the artifact, and runs the deployment script with the token in `env`.

beats.text: The textbook names four decisions worth defending in a review.
beats.tele: The textbook names four decisions worth defending in a review.

beats.text: Build once, deploy what was built. The deploy job doesn't run the build again. It downloads the artifact. Every job starts on a fresh machine, so the artifact is the only way the bytes travel, and it's also the point: the thing that was tested is the thing that is deployed. The download action at version 8 fails by default when the content doesn't match the digest recorded at upload.
beats.tele: Build once, deploy what was built. The deploy job doesn't run the build again. It downloads the artifact. Every job starts on a fresh machine, so the artifact is the only way the bytes travel, and it's also the point: the thing that was tested is the thing that is deployed. The download action at version 8 fails by default when the content doesn't match the digest recorded at upload.

beats.text: The environment belongs to the job that deploys. Only deploy-staging names it. The build job can't read the deployment token, because an environment secret is "only available to workflow jobs that reference the environment". So test code and build scripts, including those of your dependencies, never run in a job that holds a deployment credential.
beats.tele: The environment belongs to the job that deploys. Only `deploy-staging` names it. The build job can't read the deployment token, because an environment secret is "only available to workflow jobs that reference the environment". So test code and build scripts, including those of your dependencies, never run in a job that holds a deployment credential.

says: Only deploy-staging names the environment: build cannot read the deployment token

beats.text: The secret reaches the script through env. It's never interpolated into the text of a run command.
beats.tele: The secret reaches the script through `env`. It's never interpolated into the text of a `run` command.

says: Only deploy-staging names the environment: build cannot read the deployment token
The secret reaches the script through env, never in the text of a run command

beats.text: And environment.url: shown with the deployment on GitHub, taken from an environment variable, so the workflow file contains no host name.
beats.tele: And `environment.url`: shown with the deployment on GitHub, taken from an environment variable, so the workflow file contains no host name.

says: Only deploy-staging names the environment: build cannot read the deployment token
The secret reaches the script through env, never in the text of a run command
environment.url comes from an environment variable: no host name in the file

beats.text: Every job that references an environment creates a deployment object, unless deployment: false is set under environment. That form was added on the nineteenth of March 2026. Required reviewers and wait timers still apply, and it can't be combined with custom protection rules. Use it for a job that needs an environment's secrets but deploys nothing, for example an integration test against a staging database.
beats.tele: Every job that references an environment creates a deployment object, unless `deployment: false` is set under `environment`. That form was added on the nineteenth of March 2026. Required reviewers and wait timers still apply, and it can't be combined with custom protection rules. Use it for a job that needs an environment's secrets but deploys nothing, for example an integration test against a staging database.

beats.text: Workflow 9: promotion to production.
beats.tele: Workflow 9: promotion to production.

beats.text: deploy-production needs deploy-staging.
beats.tele: `deploy-production` needs `deploy-staging`.

beats.text: It has a concurrency group named production with cancel-in-progress: false. The next video explains that block. It names the environment production. Its steps are the same checkout, the same download, the same script with another argument.
beats.tele: It has a concurrency group named `production` with `cancel-in-progress: false`. The next video explains that block. It names the environment `production`. Its steps are the same checkout, the same download, the same script with another argument.

beats.text: The two deploy jobs are textually almost the same. The difference is on GitHub: each environment has a variable and a secret of the same name with different values, and only production has rules. The textbook calls this the pattern to aim for: the workflow describes the procedure, the environments hold what differs.
beats.tele: The two deploy jobs are textually almost the same. The difference is on GitHub: each environment has a variable and a secret of the same name with different values, and only `production` has rules. The textbook calls this the pattern to aim for: the workflow describes the procedure, the environments hold what differs.

beats.text: What the reviewer sees, from the documentation. Nothing of it was captured for the book, and the labels are GitHub's and may change. The run shows the job as waiting. A required reviewer opens the run, chooses to review deployments, selects the environment, and approves or rejects. A rejection fails the workflow. A job that nobody approves fails automatically after 30 days.
beats.tele: What the reviewer sees, from the documentation. Nothing of it was captured for the book, and the labels are GitHub's and may change. The run shows the job as waiting. A required reviewer opens the run, chooses to review deployments, selects the environment, and approves or rejects. A rejection fails the workflow. A job that nobody approves fails automatically after 30 days.

says: From the documentation, not captured: the job waits until a reviewer approves

beats.text: What an approval releases. The reviewer approves a job of a run, and a run is bound to one commit. The useful habit is to look at the range between what production has and what the run carries.
beats.tele: What an approval releases. The reviewer approves a job of a run, and a run is bound to one commit. The useful habit is to look at the range between what production has and what the run carries.

says: From the documentation, not captured: the job waits until a reviewer approves
An approval releases one job of one run, and a run is bound to one commit

beats.text: What the branch rule guarantees. A deployment branch rule compares the run's ref with name patterns. Since the eighth of December 2025, for runs triggered by pull_request events the ref that is evaluated is refs/pull/N/merge, and for pull_request_target it's the default branch. A rule "Selected branches: main" therefore rejects pull request runs and runs on other branches. It says nothing about review of the commits on main. That's the job of the ruleset on main, the named list of rules for that branch.
beats.tele: What the branch rule guarantees. A deployment branch rule compares the run's ref with name patterns. Since the eighth of December 2025, for runs triggered by `pull_request` events the ref that is evaluated is `refs/pull/N/merge`, and for `pull_request_target` it's the default branch. A rule "Selected branches: main" therefore rejects pull request runs and runs on other branches. It says nothing about review of the commits on `main`. That's the job of the ruleset on `main`, the named list of rules for that branch.

beats.text: A picture helps.
beats.tele: A picture helps.

beats.text: Analogy, from the textbook. An environment is the locked door of a server room with its own key cabinet inside. The job is a technician. The door has rules: someone must sign the visitor in, the visitor must come from a known department, there may be a waiting period. The keys in the cabinet are only reachable after the door has opened.
beats.tele: Analogy, from the textbook. An environment is the locked door of a server room with its own key cabinet inside. The job is a technician. The door has rules: someone must sign the visitor in, the visitor must come from a known department, there may be a waiting period. The keys in the cabinet are only reachable after the door has opened.

beats.text: The analogy breaks in one place, and it's the place that matters in an audit: the door is guarded by GitHub, not by the server room. If your cloud account also accepts credentials from somewhere else, the environment protects nothing.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks in one place, and it's the place that matters in an audit: the door is guarded by GitHub, not by the server room. If your cloud account also accepts credentials from somewhere else, the environment protects nothing.

beats.text: Now the sentence I promised, the one to say to a CTO. The gate is a combination of three things. A ruleset that forces changes to main through reviewed pull requests. An environment that accepts only main. And a required reviewer. In the textbook's words: remove any one and there is a path around the other two.
beats.tele: Now the sentence I promised, the one to say to a CTO. The gate is a combination of three things. A ruleset that forces changes to `main` through reviewed pull requests. An environment that accepts only `main`. And a required reviewer. In the textbook's words: remove any one and there is a path around the other two.

beats.text: Without the ruleset, anyone can push to main and the branch rule is satisfied. Without the branch rule, a run on any branch can ask for approval, or with no reviewer, deploy. Without the reviewer, every merge deploys on its own.
beats.tele: Without the ruleset, anyone can push to `main` and the branch rule is satisfied. Without the branch rule, a run on any branch can ask for approval, or with no reviewer, deploy. Without the reviewer, every merge deploys on its own.

beats.text: And two more conditions from section 20B.17 that sit outside all three. Administrators can bypass protection rules unless that is switched off, and whoever can edit the environment can remove the rule. And the credential itself must be bound to the environment at the cloud provider, or it also works from a laptop.
beats.tele: And two more conditions from section 20B.17 that sit outside all three. Administrators can bypass protection rules unless that is switched off, and whoever can edit the environment can remove the rule. And the credential itself must be bound to the environment at the cloud provider, or it also works from a laptop.

beats.text: Three boxes, and the security argument is in the right one. While the production job waits, there's no runner and there are no secrets.
beats.tele: Three boxes, and the security argument is in the right one. While the production job waits, there's no runner and there are no secrets.

beats.text: Into the lab.
beats.tele: Into the lab.

beats.text: Step 1: the same bytes. Replay labs/run ch20b/lab-27-2-artifact-digest.
beats.tele: Step 1: the same bytes. Replay `labs/run ch20b/lab-27-2-artifact-digest`.

beats.text: git archive only reads the repository, and it writes an archive to standard output. The digest of a file is a fingerprint computed from its bytes.
beats.tele: `git archive` only reads the repository, and it writes an archive to standard output. The digest of a file is a fingerprint computed from its bytes.

beats.text: Three digests. Which are equal? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Three digests. Which are equal? Say it out loud.

beats.text: The first two are equal, because git archive of one commit is deterministic. The third differs, because v1.1.0 is another commit. A build tool isn't always this reproducible. That's the reason to move the built file between jobs and not to rebuild it.
beats.tele: The first two are equal, because `git archive` of one commit is deterministic. The third differs, because `v1.1.0` is another commit. A build tool isn't always this reproducible. That's the reason to move the built file between jobs and not to rebuild it.

beats.text: One byte appended between "build" and "deploy". The recorded digest no longer matches: FAILED, exit status 1. This is what the download action's digest check does for you.
beats.tele: One byte appended between "build" and "deploy". The recorded digest no longer matches: FAILED, exit status 1. This is what the download action's digest check does for you.

beats.text: And the recovery has a rule in its comment: don't repair the file. Produce it again from the commit and compare.
beats.tele: And the recovery has a rule in its comment: don't repair the file. Produce it again from the commit and compare.

beats.text: Step 2: what a deployment contains. Replay labs/run ch20b/lab-27-3-deploy-range. Staging runs v1.1.0. A push to main is about to deploy the tip of main.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Assuming a gate from the line environment: production. Root cause: protection rules are properties of the environment object on GitHub, and naming a missing environment creates it without any rule.
beats.tele: Assuming a gate from the line `environment: production`. Root cause: protection rules are properties of the environment object on GitHub, and naming a missing environment creates it without any rule.

beats.text: A misspelled environment name. Root cause: the misspelling names a new, unprotected environment; there is no error.
beats.tele: A misspelled environment name. Root cause: the misspelling names a new, unprotected environment; there is no error.

beats.text: Rebuilding in the deploy job. Root cause: a second build is not guaranteed to produce the same bytes, so the deployed thing is not the tested thing.
beats.tele: Rebuilding in the deploy job. Root cause: a second build is not guaranteed to produce the same bytes, so the deployed thing is not the tested thing.

beats.text: Re-running an old deploy run. Root cause: a re-run uses the commit of the original run, so it deploys old code over new.
beats.tele: Re-running an old deploy run. Root cause: a re-run uses the commit of the original run, so it deploys old code over new.

beats.text: Treating the environment as the only production control. Root cause: it is enforced by GitHub, and credentials that also work from elsewhere bypass it.
beats.tele: Treating the environment as the only production control. Root cause: it is enforced by GitHub, and credentials that also work from elsewhere bypass it.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The textbook's case: a team serving an LLM application keeps two cloud roles. One can update the staging service, and one can update production. The production role's credentials are reachable only from the production environment, which requires one approval from the on-call group, prevents self-review and accepts only main.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. The textbook's case: a team serving an LLM application keeps two cloud roles. One can update the staging service, and one can update production. The production role's credentials are reachable only from the `production` environment, which requires one approval from the on-call group, prevents self-review and accepts only `main`.

beats.text: An engineer edits a workflow on a feature branch to "quickly deploy". The job fails the branch rule before any runner starts. The textbook's remark: the gate did its work without anybody reading the diff.
beats.tele: An engineer edits a workflow on a feature branch to "quickly deploy". The job fails the branch rule before any runner starts. The textbook's remark: the gate did its work without anybody reading the diff.

beats.text: And the next layer, which Part 7 covers: with federated credentials the same idea is enforced by the cloud provider as well, because the token's subject names the environment.
